articles.title: India pledges $1.6bn in flood relief for Nepal as Balendra Shah visits Modi
articles.summary: Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for a two-day visit — his first since coming to power in March.
articles.body:
India will provide Nepal with a $1.62bn economic package in the wake of August’s devastating floods in the country, which led to the deaths and disappearances of thousands of people.

The sum announced on Monday is one of its largest-ever relief commitments, and comes as New Delhi boosts ties with its Himalayan neighbour, where it competes with China for influence.

The announcement followed talks between India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah, who is in New Delhi for a two-day visit – his first bilateral trip abroad since coming to power in March.

“We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August,” Modi said, standing alongside Shah in New Delhi. “To support Nepal’s reconstruction, and give fresh momentum to its long-term development, we announce a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees [$1.6bn].”

August’s floods, which scientists say were caused by the effects of climate change, were triggered when part of a mountain glacier collapsed and a torrent of water and mud flooded down into Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions, as well as into China’s Tibet region on August 26. More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead, and more than 5,000 remain missing.

In October, the United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund set aside a sum of $20m for aid to Nepal.

India’s package will include a $377m grant for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects, and a $1.24bn line of credit for energy projects, the countries said in a joint statement.

India is Nepal’s largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60 percent of its imports, worth $8.6bn, while China accounts for 13 percent, or $1.8bn, according to World Bank figures.

Besides the flood relief package, the pair agreed on further cooperation in education and research, satellite communications, and sustainable urban development. The two leaders also jointly opened a train link connecting the countries.

“May the friendship between Nepal and India be one where trust stands as tall as the Himalayas,” said Shah.

articles.title: Anti-ICE protesters at Seattle-Tacoma airport force security presence during busy holiday travel
articles.summary: Video captures anti-ICE demonstrators mocking a purported "bomb technician" and cursing at Seattle-Tacoma airport police during holiday travel rush.
articles.body: Video from an anti-ICE demonstrator at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport shows him taunting the police and security presence Sunday, including his mocking the sight of a purported "bomb technician." The footage showed agitators crowding near security lines and shouting profanities at Port of Seattle police officers, whom protesters accused of acting as "collaborators." At one point in the footage, an agitator mocks the heightened security threat brought on by the demonstration. "Let’s see what we got: Ew, bomb technician: Apparently they’re worried a bunch of dirty hippies might, I don’t know," the speaker says in the video, not completing the thought before resuming chanting and cursing at police and security officers attempting to secure the airport and help innocent travelers get through the disruptions. DHS, DEM OFFICIALS CLASH AFTER ICE ARREST AT SEATTLE AIRPORT The Sunday demonstrators descended on the airport during the busy holiday travel rush, after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained two alleged visa overstayers on a Sea-Tac jetway Saturday morning. According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), one was being detained before boarding a flight, prompting another woman to object and allegedly douse federal agents with hot coffee during an Alaska Airlines boarding operation. Former Rep. Mayra Flores, R-Texas, weighed in on the controversy on X, criticizing the outrage directed at federal officers rather than the enforcement of law and order at airports during the busy travel season. NYC ICE CHIEF FIRES BACK AT FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS SEEKING TO ABOLISH AGENCY: 'CHANGE THE LAW' "You don’t get to come to America for a soccer game, overstay your visa for months, throw hot coffee at federal agents, and then expect the country to treat you like a victim," Flores, who was married to a U.S. Border Patrol agent, wrote. "If an American did that in another country, they’d face the consequences, not a governor rushing to their defense or headlines designed to make everyone feel sorry for them. "ICE was doing its job: enforcing the law. The outrage shouldn’t be directed at the agents. It should be directed at the decision to overstay and assault them," Flores added. "Enforcing the law isn’t the problem. Breaking it is." Ric Grenell, Trump administration special presidential envoy for special missions, issued a series of rebukes of the outrage and protests, noting the flouting of law and order. DHS DENOUNCES TX OFFICIALS FOR ALLEGEDLY PLANNING TO END COOPERATION WITH ICE "It’s the law," Grenell wrote Sunday on X, responding to Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who vowed that ICE "needs to be reined in before causing more chaos and fear." "Work harder to change the law – but don’t undermine our democracy by picking and choosing WHICH laws you follow." Grenell also expressed concern that the official Sea-Tac airport leadership was calling out ICE. "Seems very dangerous to fly into Seattle Tacoma Airport if they refuse to enforce Federal laws," Grenell wrote. "What other laws are they picking and choosing to ignore?" CHILD MOLESTER'S LOOMING PRISON RELEASE REIGNITES SANCTUARY SHOWDOWN IN WAKE OF DEM ELECTION SWEEP Grenell also shared concern that a flight attendant union leader was openly breaking from supporting law and order at American airports and security checkpoints. "Yikes. The union boss for flight attendants is calling for Federal laws to be ignored," Grenell wrote Sunday on X. That post shared the weekend outrage from the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA President Sara Nelson. "Get the hell out of our airports, ICE!" Taylor wrote. "@DHSgov stop your terror campaign!" "Get OUT ICE!!!" she added in another post. LAPD WARNS PARENTS ABOUT STUDENT SAFETY, SAYS '3RD PARTY ORGANIZERS' RECRUIT KIDS FOR ANTI-ICE WALKOUTS The outrage and protests came after the Saturday operation around 8:05 a.m. PT as travelers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight, according to DHS. Officials stated that ICE officers targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national accused of overstaying his visa, and subsequently arrested Sofia Hernandez Mejia after she allegedly threw hot coffee at agents interfering with the arrest. DHS stated Mejia will be charged with assaulting a federal officer. An attorney representing Mejia disputed DHS's characterization of her client's immigration status in a statement shared with Fox News. "She is not a U.S. citizen and was in the process of adjusting her status. It is pending with USCIS," attorney Olia Catala said. "Yes, her entry into the United States was lawful. She subsequently had pending asylum status, later married a U.S. citizen, and was undergoing the legal process to adjust her status." The arrests sparked immediate fury from Washington state Democrats, several of whom accused federal agents of creating chaos during one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. BUSH-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP IMMIGRATION RULE, RIPS DHS FOR OVERSTEPPING ITS AUTHORITY Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called video of the jetway arrest "horrific" and "chilling," declaring in a Saturday news conference that "ICE is completely and totally out of control." Ferguson urged Alaska Airlines representatives to "call on ICE to get out of our airports," adding he plans to make the same request to other carriers operating out of Sea-Tac. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., accused the law enforcers of terrorizing the community, comparing the incident to that of "fascist states." Smith described ICE as "operating as a paramilitary force that is a profound threat to our community," while Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson called the enforcement tactics "unacceptable and un-American." DHS pushed back against the criticism, defending the agents and pointing to what the agency described as a surge in violence against federal officers, citing DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin's directive to prosecute anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement to the fullest extent of the law. "Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them," DHS wrote on X. "This violence must end." articles.title: Hero riverboat captain describes harrowing rescue after tanker collision in New Orleans
articles.summary: Capt. Leonard Stewart recalls having 20 seconds to react before the Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck his riverboat, plunging him 50 feet into the Mississippi.
articles.body: A New Orleans riverboat captain who survived a 50-foot plunge into the Mississippi River before helping rescue stranded passengers is speaking out about the harrowing tanker collision that capsized his vessel earlier this month. "There wasn't a whole lot of time to react," Capt. Leonard Stewart told "Fox & Friends First" on Monday. "From when I... heard the horns and saw the ship coming right at us, [there were] probably about 20 seconds, and you don't have a lot of time to react. Honestly, I thought the ship was going to split the boat in half." AT LEAST 100 PEOPLE PULLED FROM MISSISSIPPI RIVER AFTER NEW ORLEANS SHIP CRASH AS LENGTHY SALVAGE EFFORT LOOMS The incident happened on Nov. 13, when an Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck the docked American Heritage vessel near the Port of New Orleans, causing the riverboat to capsize. At least 100 passengers were pulled from the Mississippi River. Everyone involved survived, though some were hospitalized following the incident. Stewart was among those thrown into the Mississippi River as the vessel overturned, plunging approximately 50 feet into the water and suffering injuries to his left leg and right foot. "When the boat capsized, it sent me into the water from about a 50-foot drop, and the fire and rescue boat was on the scene," he recalled. 'THIS WAS A MIRACLE': CRUISE PASSENGERS DESCRIBE FRANTIC ESCAPE AS TANKER STRIKES SHIP "They had me out of the water in about three minutes. And as soon as I got on board [the fireboat], I asked, what can I do? And I grabbed a pipe pole and started fishing people out of [the] water, and I stayed on that vessel until the last person had made it out," he added. Stewart said he is currently "taking it easy" after suffering the injuries and credited first responders, good Samaritans, tugboat captains and members of his crew for their heroic actions that day. Investigators are examining a possible steering issue involving the tanker, though the exact cause of the collision remains unknown. articles.title: Russia threatens ‘hostile’ Estonia with ‘open war’
articles.summary: Moscow accuses Tallinn of ‘hostile actions’ citing border closure and claiming it is allowing Ukraine to launch attacks.
articles.body:
Russia has accused Estonia of carrying out numerous “hostile actions” and threatened “open war” against the neighbouring Baltic state.

Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday accused Tallinn of a ⁠⁠range of hostile actions, asserting that the NATO and European Union member state is “on ⁠⁠the verge of triggering open war”.

The outburst comes after Estonia announced the planned closure of its border with Russia, and a Ukrainian attack on a Russian ship in the Baltic Sea.

The ministry set out its accusations in a statement after ⁠⁠summoning Estonia’s charge d’affaires in Moscow, Marek Uhtegi, to issue a formal protest over Tallinn’s decision to close the border.

“The Estonian diplomat was once again told that such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of triggering open war with Russia,” it said, adding that Estonia is displaying “Russophobic” tendencies.

Among a list of additional accusations, the ministry said Estonia had “tacitly allow[ed] its airspace to be used by Ukrainian drones for attacks on northwestern Russia”. Tallinn was swift to deny the claim.

It also accused Estonia of trying to obstruct the movement of Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea, banning the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain, seeking a ban on the Russian language and threatening to close the Russian Orthodox Church.

“The Russian side reserves the right to take comprehensive political and diplomatic measures aimed at protecting Russia’s national interests and the legitimate rights of its citizens,” the ministry said.

Estonia is host to a sizeable ethnic Russian population, which Moscow has often claimed is subject to discrimination.

Russia’s incursions into eastern Ukraine in 2014 were based on claims of suppression of Russian speakers’ rights in the region.

Earlier this month, Estonia said it would close border crossings with Russia from December 1 for at least six months, having accused the Kremlin’s security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company.

This marked a sharp escalation in tensions between Estonia and Russia, which Tallinn – Kyiv’s ally – sees as part of a broader campaign of hostile activity linked to Moscow’s war in Ukraine.

Russia has denied any involvement in the attack. Closing the border, the ministry said, “will inevitably backfire – not only on Tallinn itself but also on its allies within the EU and NATO”.

In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Estonia did not respond to all of the allegations but denied that it allows its territory to be used for Ukrainian military operations.

“While we generally do not comment on or engage with Russian propaganda narratives, in this case we can reiterate that Estonia has never allowed, and will never allow, its territory to be used for military operations by another country,” it said.

“Other countries in our region have also made this position clear,” it added.

Russia has long accused Estonia and other NATO states in the Baltic region of allowing Ukrainian drones to use their airspace. Ukrainian drones have frequently entered NATO airspace, but Kyiv says this is a result of Russian signal jamming.

NATO countries have repeatedly denied intentionally allowing drones to use their airspace, and blamed Russia for the incursions.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, speaking in Berlin, said the alliance was monitoring the situation in Estonia, along with an incursion last week by Russian missiles into Poland, adding that NATO had options available to respond.

“We see situations in Poland and Estonia, etc ,” Rutte said. “When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary.”

articles.title: Female physician assistants at Michigan Medicine allegedly earned $9,000 less a year than male colleagues; on November 20, appeals judges allowed newer equal-pay claims to proceed while barring older parts of the lawsuit
articles.summary: A $9,000 annual pay difference between female and male physician assistants has become the centre of a legal battle at Michigan Medicine, with employees
articles.body: A $9,000 annual pay difference between female and male physician assistants has become the centre of a legal battle at Michigan Medicine, with employees challenging how long they can seek compensation for alleged unequal wages. The dispute has raised an important question: can each allegedly lower paycheque be treated as a separate act of discrimination, even when the pay gap has existed for years?In an opinion issued on November 20, 2026, the Michigan Court of Appeals partially upheld and partially reversed a lower court's decision in Christine Oldenburg-McGee v. Regents of the University of Michigan. The published ruling, available on Justia, allowed claims arising from October 3, 2024, onwards to proceed against the university defendants while barring older claims that did not meet the state's six-month notice requirement. The court did not decide whether gender-based pay discrimination had actually occurred.Alleged $9,000 annual pay differenceThe lawsuit was brought by Christine Oldenburg-McGee, a physician assistant employed at Michigan Medicine. She filed the case individually and on behalf of other similarly situated female physician assistants, alleging that women received approximately $9,000 less in average annual salaries than comparable male employees. Oldenburg-McGee was also an elected leader of the United Physician Assistants of Michigan Medicine (UPAMM), a bargaining unit representing physician assistants. She had advocated for closing the alleged gender-based wage gap.In 2021, the bargaining unit negotiated a collective bargaining agreement with the university that established salaries for physician assistants. However, Oldenburg-McGee maintained that the agreement did not eliminate the disparity and instead reinforced it. She alleged that the university and other defendants knew about the pay difference but failed to correct it over several years.On April 3, 2025, she filed a notice of intent to bring a gender-discrimination class action. Twelve days later, she formally commenced the lawsuit, seeking compensation for female physician assistants who had worked at Michigan Medicine during the preceding three years. The complaint alleged financial losses involving salaries and benefits, along with emotional distress, financial stress and lost economic opportunities.Why the university challenged the lawsuitThe university defendants argued that the lawsuit was filed too late under the Michigan Court of Claims Act. The law requires individuals bringing certain claims involving personal injuries against the state to file a notice within six months of the event giving rise to the claim. They argued that the alleged pay disparity had existed since at least 2021, when the collective bargaining agreement was negotiated. Because the notice was not filed until April 2025, they maintained that the claims were already time-barred.They also relied on an earlier Michigan Supreme Court ruling rejecting the continuing violations doctrine for claims under the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act (ELCRA). Under that principle, employees cannot revive older discrimination claims simply by arguing that similar conduct continued over time. Oldenburg-McGee countered that every time a female physician assistant received a lower payment than a similarly situated male colleague, a new potential discrimination claim arose. Therefore, she argued, the latest payments were covered by the notice filed in April 2025.Appeals court draws a line at October 2024The appeals court agreed that individual underpayments could give rise to separate potential claims under the ELCRA. It explained that a wage claim generally becomes actionable when the work is performed and payday arrives. However, the court also held that the six-month notice requirement applied to claims against the university defendants. Since Oldenburg-McGee filed her notice on April 3, 2025, claims arising before October 3, 2024, could not proceed against those defendants.The judges therefore rejected the university's attempt to dismiss the entire lawsuit but agreed that the older claims had to be excluded. The ruling also distinguished the claims against the university institutions from those against individual defendants David Miller, Jovita Thomas-Williams and Hakim Berry. The court held that the six-month notice requirements did not apply to claims against these individuals in their personal capacities and said it lacked jurisdiction to review the lower court's decision concerning them.The Michigan Court of Appeals reversed the lower court in part, affirmed it in part and remanded the case for further proceedings. The decision allows the qualifying newer equal-pay claims to continue, but it does not establish that the university discriminated against female physician assistants or award them compensation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump delays explosive detonation in US state of Iowa amid legal battles
articles.summary: Iowa detonation postponed as Trump cites safety risks, lead exposure, and court rulings in Midwestern controversy.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has ordered the military to delay a planned controlled detonation of more than four tonnes of explosives in the Midwestern state of Iowa until a federal appeals court and the state’s governor sign off on it.

Trump’s announcement on Monday comes amid a string of delays and a late-stage legal challenge raised by environmental groups in Iowa over approximately 9,700 pounds of degraded lead azide stored in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this long-term problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” the president posted on his Truth Social platform.

Inside the legal fight to halt the blasts

The explosions — originally set to take place on Friday before being postponed until Monday — first hit a legal obstacle after environmental health advocacy groups, the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council, filed a petition for review and an emergency motion seeking to halt the detonation on Thursday.

They questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13, which authorised the military to move forward with the blasts under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA).

The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).

They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.

In response to the suit, the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit temporarily froze the EPA’s emergency detonation permit last week while it reviewed the case.

But in a November 21 court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.

In his Monday post, the president blamed the Obama administration for improperly storing the munitions in 2009.

Military officials have previously noted the barrels were kept at the Iowa facility — in a mixture of water and ethanol — for more than two decades.

According to a court declaration , an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form as recently as March.

The president also warned that blocking the destruction of the unstable explosive carries dire consequences — and that incoming Democratic Senator Rob Sand would be responsible should the material spontaneously detonate.

Sand, who previously criticised an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity” around the blast, has warned that blowing up the stockpile could send a toxic plume of lead dust across communities in southeastern Iowa and neighbouring Illinois. Lead is a dense metal associated with severe health risks, including birth defects .

Sand’s office did not respond to questions.

Trump further emphasised that current weather conditions are optimal for a controlled blast and framed any further delay as a choice by the courts and Iowa’s incoming leadership.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and long-term, situation,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

articles.title: Protesting Bangladesh garment workers reject pay offer
articles.summary: Bangladesh’s garment industry brings in about $38bn a year. The minimum wage is around 12,500 taka ($100) per month.
articles.body:
Representatives of Bangladeshi garment workers have rejected a pay offer from employers.

Factory owners submitted a pay proposal at a meeting convened by the government-appointed wage board on Monday, but worker representatives dismissed it as too low.

The failure to reach an agreement during the wage talks suggests that the weeks of strikes and protests over the minimum wage in the industry could persist.

Babul Akhter, who represents workers on the wage board, told reporters after the meeting that “the offer … falls far short of what we have been demanding”, according to the AFP news agency.

The board kept the figure that had been offered confidential, although Chairman Judge Syed Azad Subhani said the proposed monthly minimum wage was above 14,500 taka ($116).

Workers’ representatives had formally proposed 32,000 taka ($258) for the lowest regular pay grade and 30,000 taka ($241) for apprentices.

Bangladesh’s garment industry brings in about $38bn a year, employs around four million people, and accounts for roughly four-fifths of the country’s export earnings.

However, the world’s second-largest garment exporter after China has seen widespread protests since October. Strikes have disrupted production at factories across the country, closing around 500 of its more than 4,000 clothing factories.

Workers say that wages have failed to keep up with the rising cost of food, housing, transport and healthcare.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association estimated that 317 factories lost $428m in production between November 1 and 18.

During the last wage review in 2023, labour groups rallied for a monthly minimum of at least 23,000 taka ($185). The government set it at 12,500 taka ($100), a figure unions rejected at the time but ultimately accepted.

They are now pushing for an increase of around 140 percent, but their anger has risen due to the closure of around 500 plants by employers.

A “no work, no pay” provision in the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

articles.title: Iran flogs singer Parastoo Ahmadi for performing without headscarf
articles.summary: Ahmadi and four production team members also face two-year bans on travel and artistic activity.
articles.body:
Iran has flogged a singer and her production team after they were convicted of “offending public decency”, according to local media.

The sentence of 74 lashes handed down to Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her team was carried out in the city of Qom on Monday, the singer’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told the Emtedad news website.

A court in the city had sentenced the quintet in June. They were convicted of “producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online” over a video showing Ahmadi performing without wearing the mandatory hijab alongside male musicians.

The video was posted on YouTube in December 2024. In addition to the flogging, the five were banned for two years from taking part in artistic and musical activities and leaving Iran.

Western governments and human rights groups have condemned flogging as a form of torture that violates international law.

Iran rejects criticism of its human rights record and says Western countries should address abuses of their own.

Iran’s mandatory hijab rules became a focal point of protests in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish Iranian woman, died in custody following her arrest for allegedly violating the dress code.

More women have since defied the rules in Tehran and elsewhere in Iran, while authorities have enforced them more selectively.

articles.title: US drug prices leave patients facing impossible choices
articles.summary: Despite having jobs and health insurance, some of the US’s sickest patients have trouble affording medicines they need.
articles.body:
Sarah Wisniewski and her sister were once contemplating an extraordinary arrangement to manage their shared multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnoses: alternating months taking a life-changing medication.

The drug, which Wisniewski says costs thousands of dollars a month without insurance coverage, was so expensive that the sisters considered rationing their treatment rather than going without it entirely.

“It’s a weird thing to have to think about,” the 45-year-old told Al Jazeera. “You go to college, you get insurance, you get a good job, you pay your bills, you do everything right and, still, you’re having to ration your medication.”

Wisniewski is one of more than four in 10 adults in the United States who did not take medication as prescribed last year because of the cost, estimates KFF, an independent health policy research organisation.

Her experience highlights the growing financial pressures facing some of the nation’s sickest patients, who have trouble affording costly prescription medications, despite having jobs and private health insurance.

‘Every spare dime’ needed for medications

Wisniewski was diagnosed with MS in 2017 after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms, including difficulties with her vision, mobility and breathing.

She became one of the nearly eight in 10 American adults who are living with at least one chronic condition, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In the summer of 2024, her neurologist prescribed Kesimpta, a medication that, she says, dramatically improved her condition. But her insurance company, Blue Cross Blue Shield, notified her it would not cover the treatment.

Wisniewski appealed three times before requesting a hearing in her state of Maryland. Only weeks before that hearing was due to take place did her insurer agree to cover the medication.

Without that intervention, Wisniewski said, she would have faced a monthly bill of approximately $10,000.

The impact of obtaining treatment has been significant on her life.

“I went from barely being able to walk … Now, I walk my dog every morning, a mile-and-a-half to two miles,” she said.

Wisniewski has also been able to maintain her federal contracting job, which she described as highly technical and demanding.

But the financial burden remains substantial. Even with the help of insurance, Wisniewski estimates she spends between $800 and $900 each month on medication.

“Almost every spare dime I get is going to just keeping me healthy, so I can make it to work the next day,” she said.

Unlike many countries, particularly wealthier ones, the US allows pharmaceutical companies significantly more latitude to set their own prices.

According to the Patients For Affordable Drugs Now patient-advocacy organisation, current laws give manufacturers “unilateral power to set launch prices in the US and the ability to raise prices at will”.

“I believe this is a uniquely American problem, ”Wisniewski said. “Other countries are … able to provide for their citizens these drugs, if not for free, at an affordable level.”

The monthly cost of her medication in Canada is 2,333 Canadian dollars ($1,623). It’s even lower in Australia at 41 Australian dollars ($27) or 6.60 Australian dollars ($4.37) with a concession card, which allows eligible residents in the country to receive discounts on healthcare and prescription medicines.

The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), a consortium that represents US drug companies, argues that a complicated network of third-party middlemen, known as pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and insurance companies are to blame for the country’s high drug prices.

“PBMs and insurers control benefits through processes like prior authorisation, embedded step therapy, and formulary controls that may allow PBMs and insurers to deny coverage or push patients to alternative treatments from the initially prescribed medicine,” PhRMA’s website said. The organisation did not reply to a request for comment.

A study by the nonpartisan RAND organisation, released in 2024, found that US prescription drug prices were substantially higher than those in other wealthy countries, particularly for name-brand medications.

Using 2022 data, RAND’s researchers found that US manufacturers’ gross prices across all prescription drugs were 278 percent higher than the average prices in 33 other high-income countries. For brand-name drugs, US prices were more than four times the comparison-country average.

But the consequences of the current US system can extend far beyond the cost of individual prescriptions.

Wisniewski said the money she spends maintaining access to medication is money she cannot put toward local businesses, transportation or investments in her community.

“I really think that a lot of people, at an abstract level, understand that this could happen to anybody at any point in time,” she said. “But I don’t think that it really hits home to folks that you are legitimately one bad phone call away from losing everything.”

After this month’s historic midterm elections in the US, where Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress by wide margins, there will be few areas of agreement with Democrats’ Republican counterparts – and President Donald Trump.

But targeted reforms that address the high cost of prescriptions could be an area where both parties find common ground.

A survey conducted by Fabrizio Ward in March 2025 found more than three in four voters – including 70 percent of Trump supporters – wanted Congress to take action on reducing drug prices.

The issue was the focus of a US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday of last week, when lawmakers and healthcare experts examined how pharmaceutical companies and insurers influence pricing and access to medication.

At that November 17 hearing, witnesses highlighted several factors contributing to high prescription drug costs, including pharmaceutical patent protections and the role of PBMs.

Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now, argued that pharmaceutical companies exploit the patent system to delay competition from cheaper alternatives.

One of those practices, known as patent thicketing, involves companies securing multiple patents covering different aspects of a medication or its delivery device, potentially making it more difficult for competitors to introduce generic alternatives.

Basey told lawmakers the introduction of generic competition could substantially reduce prices, arguing a single generic competitor can lower a drug’s price by 39 percent, while six or more competitors can reduce prices by as much as 95 percent.

But other witnesses pointed to PBMs, claiming their involvement in distributing drugs can influence pricing.

The Senate panel has advanced a number of proposals to tackle the high cost of prescription drugs in the US. One of those is the bipartisan Eliminating Thickets to Improve Competition (ETHIC) Act, which would limit the practice of patent thickening, making it easier for generic drugs to enter the US market and lower costs.

“Big Pharma knows exactly what it’s doing in monopolising the US patent system: driving up drug costs for Americans while preventing generic-drug manufacturers from getting their foot in the market,” Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, one of the bill’s sponsors, said in a statement.

Wisniewski noted that while the ETHIC Act wouldn’t make her prescription “cheap”, it would be “astronomically better than what we have now”.

articles.title: Russia warns of 'preventive nuclear attack' as Medvedev claims Ukraine, NATO crossed line
articles.summary: Dmitry Medvedev claims Ukraine and NATO have crossed thresholds that could make a preventive nuclear attack by Russia possible, warning Kyiv's allies.
articles.body: Russia warned Monday that it could carry out a "preventive nuclear attack" under certain circumstances, with former President Dmitry Medvedev claiming Ukraine and NATO allies have already crossed certain thresholds that could push Moscow to consider using nuclear weapons. "The massive use of non-nuclear means that cause catastrophes makes a preventive nuclear attack by the Russian Federation possible," Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote in an article published Monday in the Moscow Journal of International Law and excerpted by the state news agency TASS. Medvedev also warned that "secret or hidden supplies of nuclear weapons from the West to Kyiv will provoke a legitimate preventive nuclear attack by Russia." MOSCOW THREATENS NUCLEAR RESPONSE OVER TINY FORTRESS WEDGED BETWEEN US ALLIES AS CLASH FEARS GROW "Kyiv and its allies must remember that the Russian Federation not only has the right, but in various situations has the obligation to use nuclear weapons," he wrote. Medvedev's warning came amid continuing tensions between Moscow and the West over the nearly five-year war in Ukraine and NATO's military support for Kyiv. He argued that Ukraine and its Western allies have already created circumstances under which Russia could consider a nuclear strike, though he said Russian President Vladimir Putin carefully weighs the consequences before making such a decision. "Formally, in a number of cases, the parties collectively opposing us (Ukraine, NATO countries, and several Western countries outside the alliance) have already created situations in which Russia considers the possibility of launching a nuclear strike," Medvedev wrote in the article, titled "State Sovereignty and Nuclear Weapons: International Legal Aspects of Ensuring National Security". TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL Despite those warnings, Medvedev wrote that Putin "is always guided by a comprehensive analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage inflicted and the retaliatory measures." Medvedev also said Russia has not used nuclear weapons during the war with Ukraine because it has not considered them necessary, though he warned that calculation could change. "Obviously, so far the course of events in the Ukrainian crisis has not created a state of direct necessity to use nuclear weapons," he wrote. "The decision on Russia's use of nuclear weapons during the special military operation was not taken due to the lack of a direct necessity to do so," he added, using the Kremlin's preferred term for the war in Ukraine. Medvedev argued that while Russia's nuclear doctrine does not explicitly authorize preventive nuclear strikes, certain scenarios — including catastrophic attacks using conventional weapons or the transfer of nuclear arms to Ukraine — could justify preemptive action. He said any final decision rests solely with Putin. TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE "In making such decisions, the Russian president is always guided by a complete analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage caused and the retaliatory measures," Medvedev wrote. "The Kyiv regime and its sponsors must not harbor dangerous illusions," he warned. "If the scenarios mentioned above were to occur, the head of state not only has the right, but also the obligation to use nuclear weapons. All those who are currently fanning the flames must fully realize this". Medvedev's remarks came within days of President Donald Trump meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Nov. 19 in Shenzhen, China, where the leaders of the three nuclear powers agreed to pursue talks aimed at reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation. While the summit produced no major breakthrough on arms reductions, the leaders reaffirmed in a declaration that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER To support his argument, Medvedev cited a 1996 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, contending that international law does not categorically prohibit the use of nuclear weapons when a state's survival is at stake. The court concluded that the threat or use of nuclear weapons would generally violate international humanitarian law, but it did not definitively resolve whether such use would be lawful in extreme circumstances of self-defense. Medvedev, who served as Russia's president from 2008 to 2012 and later as prime minister under Putin, has become one of Moscow's most outspoken voices on nuclear escalation since Russia invaded Ukraine. Medvedev accused NATO members of undermining nonproliferation efforts, criticizing Germany's participation in nuclear deterrence arrangements and arguing that NATO's nuclear-sharing policies do not represent a universally accepted interpretation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On Monday, he also accused the U.S. of applying double standards toward Iran and said Washington used nonproliferation fears to justify military action against Tehran while following its own objectives.

articles.title: Betsi Cadwaladr health board bosses 'lost interest' in patients
articles.summary: Patients describe days waiting in A&E at a health board in special measures for almost a decade.
articles.body:
A woman who spent 48 hours desperately unwell in an emergency department corridor says bosses at Wales' biggest health board have lost interest in patients.

Jo Hughes, 72, who is in remission from cancer, spent two days in a hospital chair with Covid, pneumonia and a kidney infection.

Another patient, who has been treated at the same hospital for 30 years, said the north Wales health board Betsi Cadwaladr is "completely leaderless" and has declined "beyond redemption".

A report into the health board's culture and leadership is expected later.

After her experience at Ysbyty Glan Clwyd in Denbighshire, Hughes said: "I'm not going back to that after what I've been through."

The review was commissioned by the Welsh government in the summer, after it gave Betsi Cadwaladr a "final chance" to improve following nine years in special measures.

Earlier this month, the health board's chief executive Carol Shillabeer announced she was leaving in the new year to take up an NHS role in England.

Her departure follows a string of other senior leaders who have left the organisation in recent months, including the chief operating officer and executive director of finance.

Some patients blame senior managers for repeated failures.

Hughes, from Abergele, Conwy, was admitted to A&E on her doctor's advice last month.

"I didn't know what was happening to me. I didn't know what I'd got," she said.

"I felt awful. The best way I can describe it - it was a nightmare that I'd like to forget."

As the hours and days passed, she described "looking round to see if there was something spare that you could lie on".

She said: "I think it's the higher-ups. It's not the people on the ground, it's the chief executives, it's the bosses in my opinion. They're not doing their jobs."

Hughes said frontline staff were doing their best, but "the top people have lost interest".

The experience frightened her so much, she said she would refuse to go back to A&E.

"I would, honestly. I would say 'I'm not going, give me something here and now….I'm not going back to that after what I've been through'."

She also fears for older patients who might face the same experience, adding: "They wouldn't stand a chance.

"How could you have an 80 or 90-year-old sitting in a chair for 48 hours? It's ridiculous. No blankets, nothing like that. You're just plonked."

John Cooke, 78, a retired assistant chief constable with North Wales Police, was diagnosed with Crohn's disease in 1995, and was first hospitalised with it in 1996.

Regular flare-ups mean he has been admitted to Ysbyty Glan Clwyd two to three times every year over the past three decades. While he says frontline staff continue to do their best, conditions had deteriorated overall.

"I suppose the most obvious thing is the time it takes to be seen, and certainly the time it takes to be allocated to a ward and to a bed," he said.

"When I first started on this road I could certainly be in a ward, in a bed within an hour. Now, more recently, it can be very lengthy waits, despite the pain, and I recently had a 47-hour wait in A&E before I was even seen by a doctor.

"I know of people who have waited almost a week to be allocated a bed, and very seriously ill people are not exempt from these waits at all."

He was once guaranteed quarterly outpatient appointments, but said "the treatment I'm getting now as an outpatient is almost non-existent".

Cooke says he does not believe things will improve without a "complete restructuring of the organisation".

"I blame the management. Not necessarily the board because they don't have direct access to the workforce... but the management, the senior management, the executives, they are to blame. It's completely leaderless."

He said frontline staff "work so hard and continue to labour under these conditions".

articles.title: Venezuelan illegal immigrant arrested in Utah after soliciting assassination of Trump, DHS says
articles.summary: DHS says an FBI tip led to the arrest of a Venezuelan national in Provo, Utah, over stickers urging the assassination of President Donald Trump.
articles.body: An illegal immigrant was arrested in Utah last month after an investigation linked him to the distribution of images encouraging the assassination of President Donald Trump, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced Monday. Hector Alejandro Mujica-Hernandez, a Venezuelan national living in the U. S. illegally, was taken into custody in Provo. Authorities said the arrest followed a tip from the FBI regarding online assassination threats against Trump that were traced back to Mujica-Hernandez's activity. SECRET SERVICE ARRESTS ARMED VENEZUELAN MIGRANT NEAR WHITE HOUSE OVER ALLEGED TRUMP ASSASSINATION THREAT "This illegal alien not only broke our laws by illegally overstaying his visa, but threatened the life of the President of the United States," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. "The Department of Homeland Security will not tolerate death threats of any kind." According to DHS, the investigation centered on stickers distributed during a meeting of a group called "People of Provo Against ICE" (POPAI). The stickers featured rhetoric supporting Trump's assassination, including the phrase: "Shoot Trump, be a hero, become unforgettable." DHS noted that the letter "A" on the stickers was stylized as an upside-down anarchist symbol commonly associated with Antifa and anarchist groups. EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET Trump has been the subject of several assassination plots, while U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have faced an uptick in attacks amid the administration's immigration enforcement agenda. "The media and the far-left must stop vilifying ICE law enforcement officers and President Trump," said Mullin, casting blame on both for threats and attacks against ICE and Trump. articles.title: Appeals court OKs Army plan to blow up tons of lead-based explosives in Iowa, hours after Trump put it on hold
articles.summary: The blast risks sending a plume of toxic particles into nearby communities, but the Army says a controlled explosion is the safest way to deal with the highl...
articles.body:
A federal appeals court cleared the way for the U.S. Army to detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead-based explosives stored at a facility in Iowa on Monday, hours after President Trump announced that he had halted the plan. The court's order is the latest twist in an ongoing controversy over the military's effort to dispose of the volatile material in a controlled explosion before it potentially detonates on its own.

Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday morning that, while he believes the "proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem," he would not allow the Army to destroy the material until federal courts sign off on the plan and Iowa's Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand gives his approval.

It's unclear whether Trump will continue to insist on Sand's sign-off before allowing the detonation, which had been scheduled for Wednesday, to be carried out.

The explosion threatens to send a plume of toxic lead dust over local communities, livestock and farmland in the surrounding area. Environmentalists sued to stop the detonation last week, setting off a back-and-forth legal battle. The military has argued that the controlled detonation must take place soon, before impending cold weather potentially causes the material to combust on its own.

Here's what led to the current situation, what the dangers are and what might happen next.

The roots of the controversy reportedly date back to at least March, when the Army discovered nearly 5 tons of deteriorating lead azide, a dangerous bomb-making material, stored at an ammunition plant in rural Iowa. According to legal filings , the lead azide had crystallized over the course of two decades, leaving it highly susceptible to exploding. The material is so volatile, the Army says, that the friction and motion of attempting to move it somewhere safer would likely cause it to explode.

According to the New York Times, the Army at first hired a chemical company to carry out a process that could neutralize the material without an explosion, but later determined that detonating it was the right course of action.

Earlier this month, the Environmental Protection Agency approved an emergency permit allowing the Army to carry out a controlled detonation of the lead azide.

The detonation was initially scheduled to take place on Friday. But local environmental groups filed a lawsuit aiming to stop the plan from going forward, arguing that the EPA failed to apply proper environmental standards when it approved the detonation, creating the risk of "immediate, irreparable harm" to surrounding communities.

On Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an order temporarily blocking the Army from carrying out the detonation. But the Army argued in a filing Saturday that the situation has become so dangerous that it has the authority to proceed under a separate emergency exemption.

The blast was on track to happen on Wednesday until Trump intervened. The court issued its ruling allowing the detonation to proceed about five hours after Trump's post was published.

Lead is a neurotoxin that poses a serious risk to those who are exposed to it, particularly pregnant women and young children. No one disputes that blowing up the barrels of lead azide could release dangerous material to the surrounding area. The Army shared modeling showing lead particles from the explosion traveling as far as 40 miles and airborne dust drifting up to 100 miles.

The American Lung Association has advised people in the area to stay indoors for 24 to 48 hours after the blast to avoid exposure.

The Army argues that, whatever risks the planned detonation poses, doing nothing creates the danger of something much worse.

The real choice … is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion," the government wrote in a legal filing .

But environmental groups have countered that the public was only given a few days' notice before the initial planned detonation, not nearly enough time for local residents to understand the full scope of the risk and take the steps they need to stay safe.

The groups also questioned how the Army allowed the situation to become so urgent when it had been aware of the material for at least eight months. Sand echoed that sentiment in a post on social media on Sunday.

"No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been," he wrote on X . "Most clearly, since a contract to remove explosive risk was signed this spring, we must all be asking why it was cancelled, why nothing was done, and why we are rushing to demolition now in late November."

Officials haven't yet said whether the plan to detonate the material on Wednesday remains in place and Trump hasn't clarified whether he will still seek Sand's approval in the wake of the court's filing.

articles.title: Drone attack on police base in Colombia injures three, including infant
articles.summary: Far-right President De la Espriella steps up offensive as rebel groups strike back with drone strikes, roadside bombs.
articles.body:
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.

Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.

Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.

The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.

Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.

Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.

In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.

However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.

Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.

Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

articles.title: UK weather: Cold spell continues with risk of hill snow, ice and heavy rain
articles.summary: Colder weather continues for much of the UK with some ice and hill snow but milder and wetter in the south and west, as Simon King explains
articles.body:
As the coldest spell of the autumn so far continues, parts of the UK could see some hill snow, ice or heavy rain this week.

With Arctic air to the north and east of the UK, Scotland, northern and eastern England will experience temperatures below the average with some hill snow, freezing rain and ice.

Meanwhile, milder air to the west of the UK will bring heavy rain to parts of Northern Ireland, Wales and south-west England with temperatures around average.

The battle between colder and milder conditions is likely to continue through the week.

It will be a cold and frosty start to the day across Scotland, northern and eastern areas of England with temperatures in the morning starting below freezing.

There will be some rain, however, moving in from the south-west early on Tuesday that will mix with colder air and bring some wintry hazards.

Over the higher ground of the North Pennines, Cheviots, Southern Uplands and Grampians, there may be a spell of freezing rain.

Freezing rain occurs when precipitation starts off as snow coming out of cloud before it hits a milder layer of air where it melts into liquid rain.

What is freezing rain? Published 17 February 2025

How to stay safe when driving in the snow

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips

It then passes through another colder layer of air - below freezing - close to the ground. On hitting surfaces such as the road, pavement, cars or power lines, the liquid rain freezes instantly to create a layer of ice.

In prolonged periods, it can be one of the most hazardous types of winter weather, especially in built up and populated areas.

For the rest of Tuesday, there could be a few centimetres of snow over the higher ground of the Grampians.

Heavy rain to bring localised flood risk

While wintry hazards will affect more northern and eastern areas of the UK, in the south and west it will be milder and wetter.

Heavy rain will persist across south-west England, Wales and, for a time, Northern Ireland.

The Met Office has issued a yellow weather warning for rain covering Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly beginning at 10:00 GMT on Tuesday and lasting until 23.59 GMT.

Around 30-40mm of rain are forecast widely in the warning area, but as much as 60-90mm are possible where the heavy rain persists, particularly in western Cornwall.

Localised flooding is possible, leading to difficult driving conditions and road closures in some places.

Strong winds will develop around western areas of the UK throughout Tuesday too.

Temperatures will hold up at around 10 to 13C, which is around, if not slightly above, average for the end of November.

For the rest of the week the colder air will push back westward.

On Wednesday morning there will be some fog or freezing fog patches, especially in Northern Ireland which may be stubborn to clear.

Otherwise it will be a largely dry day with some bright or sunny spells at times.

Colder but mostly dry weather will continue into Friday before another weather system tries to make inroads to the west or south-west of the UK.

Rain will move slowly eastward and temporarily turn to snow over the hills of northern England.

articles.title: Amazon drone delivering shampoo snags on wire and tumbles onto Michigan man’s garage roof
articles.summary: James Brennan, of Huntington Woods, Michigan, near Detroit, said he had not requested a drone delivery and assumed his package would arrive at his doorstep as usual.
articles.body: When James Brennan was waiting for his shampoo delivery last week, he didn’t realize an Amazon drone would hit a wire and tumble onto the roof of his garage. Brennan, of Huntington Woods, Michigan, near Detroit, said he had not requested a drone delivery and assumed his package would arrive at his doorstep as usual. But on Friday, he received a notification from Amazon telling him to keep an eye out for the unmanned aircraft, so he went outside to take a video. “I just thought it would make amusing, amusing conversation over Thanksgiving or at work or whatever,” Brennan said in an interview. “And I was just going to get a shot of it. I never expected this to happen.” He went to the front yard and heard the unmistakable whirling of a drone as it neared. The rotors kicked up leaves, debris and dust, Brennan said, before the drone set the package down and began its ascent again. Video taken from across the street shows the drone hitting a cable, wobbling and ultimately plopping down on Brennan’s roof. “It swayed a couple of times, and then it swayed over the top of the garage,” Brennan said. “It kind of laid down and died. And as soon as it laid down, the motors shut off, and that was it.” Amazon workers responded to the incident quickly and retrieved the problem drone, but the ordeal did cause neighbors to temporarily lose internet access, he said. In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Jack Stelzner said safety is the company’s “top priority” and that “incidents are extremely rare.” “Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service,” he said. A spokesman for the National Transportation Safety Board said officials are gathering information and have not decided whether to launch an investigation. Brennan said the damage to his garage roof was “very minor,” comprising only a few scuffed shingles. He said he and some neighbors also got a $100 Amazon gift card for their troubles. Brennan now hopes Amazon will continue to refine its drone delivery system to prevent future accidents. “Until they develop better technology to spot these these kinds of things, this is going to continue to happen,” he said.

articles.title: Timms report to suggest faster Pip payments for some disabled people
articles.summary: The Timms review will recommend those with severe conditions will not need to be reassessed to receive Pip.
articles.body:
A review into the main disability benefit is set to recommend that those with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses should get quicker payments.

The report on Personal Independence Payment (Pip), which will be published on Tuesday afternoon, will also suggest that assessments are overhauled to provide claimants in England and Wales with more appropriate support.

But despite the cost of the benefit projected to more than double between 2020 and 2030, the review is understood not to suggest major savings.

Groups representing disabled people - who had a hand in drafting the report - have broadly welcomed its findings.

The review, chaired by the Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, was asked by the government to explore how the benefit, claimed by around four million people, could be made "fair and fit for the future in a changing world".

The review was set up last year after the Starmer government's aborted attempt to cut welfare spending.

Sir Stephen set out several proposals in an article in the Times on Monday, which are likely to be accepted by ministers.

These include that disability benefit payments should be linked to real-life needs and the extra costs incurred by the claimant, rather than their diagnosis.

As part of that, those with the most severe and persistent conditions would be fast-tracked with no further assessments involved - believed to be the case for about one in 10 claimants. The aim, wrote Sir Stephen, was to create a process that was "less burdensome".

The government is set to spend £32.1bn on Pip this financial year, a figure that is projected to rise to £41.5bn in 2030-31. In 2019-20, the year before the pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn, when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

"Disability claims have risen fastest amongst young people who are the least likely to be become seriously ill as a result of the pandemic," said Matt Ryder, a policy consultant with the free-market think tank the Adam Smith Institute.

"We need to target lower-level mental health claims. That seems to be the root cause of the rising claims, so we need to restrict eligibility for that."

Research last month from the Resolution Foundation, a think tank focused on lower and middle earners, suggested about one in six Pip recipients said they didn't incur any extra costs due to their disability.

The think tank suggests removing Pip from this group would save up to £4.4m a year.

Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high

Welfare cuts: What's been happening with Pip and universal credit?

'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review

Lindsay Judge, research director at the Resolution Foundation, said although the Timms Review did not set out to cut costs, "they should be possible nonetheless".

"The Timms Review rightly stated this summer that the current system of Pip is not fit for purpose, and that major change is needed.

"In its final report, the review must set out clearly how the system can work better. This should include assessments that seek to better understand disabled people's needs; awards - either through cash or services - that better reflect the actual costs that disabled people face; and more regular light touch check-ins so that changes of circumstances are fully understood."

Ryder said fewer reassessments for people with deteriorating conditions, and making the process more accessible were "individually the right thing for disabled people" but that the think tank were concerned abut the rising costs of Pip.

"The cost at the moment is acceptable, but it's where the cost is heading. The number of claimants has roughly doubled since before the pandemic. According to the OBR, we can expect that spending on Pip will rise to £47bn in five years' time. And there's no reason why it would stop at that point. Why wouldn't it continue on growing?"

The proposals will be put forward by a steering group, led by Sir Stephen, which the government will respond to.

There were concerns from disability charities that Pip payments might become means-tested or the cash payments partially replaced with vouchers, but it is understood this will not be the case.

James Taylor, head of strategy at disability charity Scope, said the organisation agreed Pip assessments needed an overhaul.

"Disabled people have told us the process is stressful and degrading. Fast-tracking claims and ending unnecessary reassessments for people with severe conditions could make a real difference.

"A better assessment should recognise the extra costs disabled people face, and should include what they need and what they are already going without. If you can't afford the taxi you need because public transport is inaccessible, the cost hasn't gone away. People need reliable cash support they can use as their needs change, whether they're in work or out of work."

'The process is intimidating and confusing'

Alicia Cartwright in Preston receives the higher rate of Pip for both the daily living and mobility components, which she says equates to about £500 every four weeks.

Cartwright is a power wheelchair user and works several part-time jobs at a university.

She says the costs of her disabilities run to a further £1,500 a month which she has to pay out of her wages.

"The mobility part of it, that goes on paying for my wheelchair. And then the rest of my Pip goes entirely on paying someone to help me around the house"

The mum of two is a trained benefits advisor, but says even she finds the current assessment process "intimidating and confusing".

"Trust disabled people to know what their needs are. Of course, have some checks in there, absolutely, but we really need to start from a place of trust.

"Currently, in any dealings with the benefits system, you feel like you're on trial, and for a lot of people, asking for help is difficult in the first place."

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales, but the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

articles.title: Israel leadership rivals clash over Iran threat
articles.summary: Gadi Eisenkot, who is tasked with forming the next Israeli govt, said he saw no immediate reason for attacking Iran Monday, contradicting caretaker PM
articles.body: Gadi Eisenkot, who is tasked with forming the next Israeli govt, said he saw no immediate reason for attacking Iran Monday, contradicting caretaker PM Benjamin Netanyahu who warned against downplaying "grave threats".The remarks from both politicians came hours before their parties were due to meet for the third time to discuss possible coalition-building, after lengthy negotiations the day before delivered no breakthrough. Eisenkot has until Dec 6 - a deadline which can be extended by 14 days - to form a govt. Netanyahu has repeatedly pressed for a unity govt, which he says is needed to guarantee Israel's security.During a press briefing at Israel's parliament in Jerusalem Monday, Eisenkot said the "Iranian threat is the most serious threat to the State of Israel". "But at this moment I do not see a direct and immediate threat to the State of Israel that would require action before a government is formed," he added. Netanyahu in turn played up the need for unity "in the face of the great threats surrounding us". "Anyone who belittles or downplays these immediate, serious and grave threats surrounding us does so for political reasons," he said in televised remarks.Delegations from Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and Netanyahu's right-wing Likud are due to meet Monday evening for a third round of negotiations, spokespeople for Likud and Yashar told AFP. Representatives from each party met for four hours Sunday and laid out their positions "on a range of substantive issues," but with no sign of a breakthrough.(This is an AFP copy)You use AI every day. articles.title: James Carville warns Gavin Newsom faces California baggage in potential 2028 run
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville says Gavin Newsom faces a major 2028 hurdle in that voters are weary of "California" style coastal politics.
articles.body: Democratic strategist James Carville suggested that California Gov. Gavin Newsom will have to reckon with Americans weary of liberal coastal politics if he runs in 2028. Speaking on the Politicon podcast with political adviser Mark McKinnon Friday, Carville weighed in on potential contenders for the 2028 Democratic nomination. When asked about Newsom’s chances, he argued that one key issue stands in his way. "Well, his strength is he runs the biggest state. He's got a huge fundraising base. There's no doubt about it. If you’re the governor of California, you could raise a lot of money," Carville said. "His problem is, ‘Are we going to do this California sh-- again? Really? Is that what we're going to do?’" "He's got to overcome that kind of barrier," Carville warned, suggesting many voters are wary of an "uber coastal candidate" leading the country. NEWSOM ROASTED ONLINE FOR 'STAGED' FLY-FISHING INTERVIEW WITH CNN ANCHOR WHERE HE DROPPED MAJOR 2028 HINT McKinnon said he was initially skeptical that Newsom might be "a little too slick, a little too Hollywood," but was impressed after interviewing him several times on his own podcast. "I mean, he's got chops," McKinnon said. Carville agreed that Newsom is quick on his feet and possesses real political skill, noting that navigating California's Democratic politics is far more difficult than outsiders assume. He also credited Newsom for being authentic to his roots, comparing the governor's California persona to his own Louisiana identity. NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’ "To his credit, he's a real California guy," he said. "He don't try to fake it." Other party insiders remain skeptical of Newsom's national appeal. Veteran Democratic strategist Doug Schoen suggested that "Gavin Newsom has no clear identity. Some days he's a moderate Bill Clinton type and on other days he tries to be a progressive — for example, he's for a national wealth tax, and he has recently commuted the sentences of hundreds of death row inmates." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "His strengths are that he's telegenic, quick on his feet and engaging," Schoen added. "His weaknesses are that he has no clear message or strategy, and that he goes whichever way the wind blows." Still, Schoen acknowledged Newsom is a serious contender because of his fundraising power and home-state base. Although Newsom has previously said he would not run if former Vice President Kamala Harris enters the race, Schoen said the governor appears eager to launch a campaign of his own. "This seems like a warning shot towards Kamala, as there is every indication that he's chomping at the bit to run himself."

articles.title: 'We will not be abused': Singapore PM Wong warns firms as Megaspeed probe continues
articles.summary: Singapore is investigating whether Megaspeed, a company linked to the Nvidia chip diversion controversy, breached local laws.
articles.body: Singapore is investigating whether Megaspeed, a company linked to the Nvidia chip diversion controversy, breached local laws. Prime minister Lawrence Wong confirmed the ongoing investigation on Monday, as he rejected concerns that the city-state was being used to circumvent US export controls.Speaking at a joint press conference with Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese in Canberra, Wong said Singapore was working with American authorities but stressed that its investigation was focused on possible violations of Singaporean law.“We do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America's export controls,” Wong said.“What we do is to facilitate checks by America to enforce its own laws. At the same time, we are also very clear we do not want companies to breach Singapore laws.”Wong's remarks came after a reporter questioned whether Singapore had become a weak link in the movement of advanced chips to China.The Singaporean prime minister said authorities had investigated Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company, as well as Alice Huang, who has been suspected by the US of links to Chinese intelligence.“We were investigating Megaspeed, which is Singapore-based entity. And we also were investigating Alice Huang herself,” Wong said.“We took her in, we investigated her, but we eventually released her because there was no basis for further prosecution. America understands what we have done.”He said Singapore had sought information from the US during its inquiries, but not all of it had been provided.“We did ask for some information, not all of it was forthcoming, but we did what we did with her, and the investigations with Megaspeed are ongoing,” Wong said.Wong later reiterated that the investigation into Megaspeed was continuing, with Singapore seeking further details from Washington to verify documents.“We are continuing to have discussions with American authorities … to confirm the verification of various documents, but these investigations into Megaspeed are ongoing,” he said.“We are focusing on whether Megaspeed might have breached any Singapore laws.”Wong also distanced Singapore from the US investigation into Huang's conduct and the question of whether Nvidia's technology had inadvertently assisted China's artificial intelligence development.“With regards to Jensen Huang's role, we are not involved in those investigations, it's for the American government to decide, and we leave them to make those investigations and judgment,” he said.“Nvidia's board will have to do what it needs to do … President Trump has already spoken, they may still be ongoing checks.”He added that Singapore would continue its own investigations into companies suspected of breaching local laws.“We are partner with the US. We are continuing to do our own investigations where it comes to companies breaching our own laws. We are very clear about that.”Wong also said no single country could determine the rules governing global artificial intelligence, as the debate over advanced chips and AI governance continues.Albanese said Australia was concerned about the issue but was not directly involved in the matter.The two leaders were in Canberra for talks aimed at strengthening bilateral ties. Albanese said Australia and Singapore shared “deep trust” built over six decades of cooperation, and announced agreements on essential supplies and transboundary carbon capture and storage.You use AI every day. articles.title: Long road from West Bengal to Paschim Banga via Bangla
articles.summary: KOLKATA: The West Bengal cabinet approved Monday a proposal to rename the state \"Paschim Banga\" in English and other Indian languages, aligning it with
articles.body: KOLKATA: The West Bengal cabinet approved Monday a proposal to rename the state "Paschim Banga" in English and other Indian languages, aligning it with the name and pronunciation that has always been used in official communication in Bengali.The BJP govt will table a resolution on this in the assembly on Dec 9 and, once it is passed, send the proposal to the Union govt, CM Suvendu Adhikari said after the cabinet meeting.Under Article 3 of the Constitution, renaming a state does not require a constitutional amendment. It can be done through legislation passed by a simple majority in both Houses of Parliament, following a recommendation from the President.With the BJP-led NDA enjoying a comfortable majority in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, the governing coalition has the numbers to get such a bill passed without a hitch.BJP's push for Paschim Banga serves both ideological and administrative purposes. Unlike the name "Bangla", which was proposed by the erstwhile Trinamool Congress govt and opposed by BJP as it sounded identical to Bangladesh, Paschim Banga preserves memories of the Partition.In June 2023, the NDA govt declared that June 20 would be observed as Bengal's Foundation Day (West Bengal Day or Paschim Banga Divas) to mark the state assembly's vote on that day in 1947 in favour of partitioning the province and creating West Bengal as a homeland for Bengali Hindus within India.By retaining the word "Paschim", BJP is seen as aiming to anchor the state's identity to the fallout of Partition and distance it from cross-border cultural overlap with Bangladesh.Alphabetically, changing the first initial in English from "W" to "P" would push Bengal up the list of states by eight notches, from the very bottom (28) to 20. This will put the state ahead of Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Tripura, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh, allowing its representatives to speak much earlier at national meetings.Over the past 27 years, the state has sent four renaming proposals to Delhi - in 1999 (when NDA was in office), 2011 (during Congress-led UPA's tenure), and in 2016 and 2018. All four proposals failed to secure the Centre's nod.In July 1999, the then Left Front govt wanted to rename the state "Bangla". In Sept 2011, the former Trinamool govt proposed that the state be known as Paschim Banga in all languages. In Aug 2016, the TMC govt got a resolution passed by the assembly proposing that the state be known as "Bangla" in Bengali, "Bengal" in English and "Bangal" in Hindi. The Union home ministry rejected the proposal on the grounds that a state must have only one name.Addressing the objection in July 2018, the assembly unanimously proposed that the state's name be changed to "Bangla" in all three languages.
