articles.title: Future of secret $1.6bn AI data centre that Wisconsin mayor stopped after residents’ protest hangs in balance as new mayor refuses …
articles.summary: The future of a $1.6 billion data centre proposal in Menomonie, western Wisconsin, remains unclear as the city’s new mayor says he will not negotiate any
articles.body: The future of a $1.6 billion data centre proposal in Menomonie, western Wisconsin, remains unclear as the city’s new mayor says he will not negotiate any development agreements with the firm behind the project. Previous mayor Randy Knaack, after listening to concerns about the project from members of the community, banned the data center project. This comes even though the city council has already annexed and rezoned about 320 acres of farmland for it. This is similar to another data centre dispute involving homeowner Jerry Zelenka who turned down a $131,000 offer from American Transmission Company (ATC). The money was offered for a proposed power line that would cross his property in Fredonia, Wisconsin, to supply electricity to a planned data centre in nearby Port Washington.‘Council tries to rebuild trust’After last year’s controversy, the Menomonie City Council has been trying to win back public trust. It has held several public meetings in recent months to gather community input. It is also considering new data centre restrictions, which would add to the ordinance passed in January.This summer, the city’s new mayor, Matthew Crowe, issued a press release saying the representatives of Balloonist, the company behind the proposal, had contacted city staff. That could suggest the company is willing to revisit the project. Crowe said he declined to meet them “to avoid being unduly influenced”.Residents’ push to stop the project has largely worked, but its fate is far from settled, as per a report by The Guardian published earlier this month. Officially, the development is paused. Balloonist, however, still owns the land.What the old mayor saidIn September last year, mayor Randy Knaack banned the construction of the data centre, and later in his “Mayor’s Report”, the mayor drafted a memo on September 17, and had the city administrator send it to Balloonist LLC.“In the document, I stated that I am not currently interested in pursuing a tax increment district or development agreement as the chief executive officer of Menomonie,” Knaack said, adding that after hearing the community’s concerns, “the data center is now on pause.”Elsewhere in Wisconsin: homeowner rejects $131,000 offer over data centre power lineAnother data centre dispute in the state centres on homeowner Jerry Zelenka. He turned down a $131,000 offer from American Transmission Company (ATC). The money was offered for a proposed power line that would cross his property in Fredonia, Wisconsin, to supply electricity to a planned data centre in nearby Port Washington.What the proposal would mean for his landZelenka, 75, said the latest plan would clear mature trees, demolish six buildings and put a 130-foot transmission tower near his driveway. He and his wife bought the land in 1990. According to Zelenka, ATC’s latest proposal follows an earlier application that the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin deemed incomplete. The company has since filed a new application with revised plans and routes.He said a stretch of about 1,000 feet long and 75 feet wide would be cleared of trees and vegetation. The trees include cedar, oak, ash, elm and black walnut. The project would also require removing a shed, chicken coop, hog barn, antique barn, garage and machine shed.“The point is that everything from that fence all the way to the road is clear-cut,” Zelenka said. “And after they clear-cut it, then they want to spray herbicide and just kill everything between my house and the highway.”The tower and high-voltage lines would also change the property’s surroundings, which could affect its value.Why he is saying noATC has offered $81,000 for the property impacts, plus a one-time $50,000 payment if he signs an agreement now. Zelenka said the compensation would not cover the cost of replacing the buildings or properly account for the loss in the property’s value. He also objected to the extra payment being tied to signing immediately.“You know, the bribe in a sense is that if I were to sign up now, they’re offering $50,000 more,” Zelenka said.He said moving is not a realistic option for him and his 73-year-old wife, who has advanced Parkinson’s disease. The couple built their home after buying the land in the winter of 1990, spending nine months on the house while living in a shed.Fearless legend or grounded realist?
